background: Background: Feb. 21, Change Healthcare, a division of UnitedHealth Group Inc. that processes insurance claims and pharmacy requests for more than 340,000 physicians and 60,000 pharmacies announced that they were hit with a cyberattack that disrupted several of its systems and services
malicious_activity:
Malicious Activity:
The hack was discovered on Feb. 21, prompting UnitedHealth to isolate the impacted systems. Change Healthcare have not provided much detail on attack itself but disclosed in February that a cyber threat actor breached part of the unit’s information technology network. The company had previously said it suspected nation-state linked hackers. BlackCat, also known as ALPHV, is one of the more prolific ransomware gangs. The Russian-speaking cybercriminal gang said on its darkweb site that it exfiltrated 6 TB of data in the attack against Change Healthcare, a unit of UnitedHealth Group’s Optum subsidiary.
outcomes_and_losses:
Outcome and Losses:
Cyber Extortion Expenses: On March 1, a Bitcoin address connected to AlphV received 350 bitcoins in a single transaction, or close to $22 million based on exchange rates at the time that looks very much like a large ransom payment.
Business Interruption & Additional Expense: Hospital procedures impacted, include insurance verification for inpatient stays, precise cost estimates and patient billing. The company also disconnected the affected systems “immediately upon detection” of the threat, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The interruptions left many health-care providers temporarily unable to fill prescriptions or get reimbursed for their services by insurers which ground revenue cycles to a halt.
Incident Response Expenses: UnitedHealth introduced its temporary funding assistance program to help providers in need of support and has paid out more than $3.3 billion to providers affected by the cyberattack on its subsidiary Change Healthcare. The company said the $3.3 billion in advances will not need to be repaid until claims flows return to normal. Federal agencies like the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services have introduced additional options to ensure that states and other stakeholders can make interim payments to providers.
